newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan orders Cambodia evacuation planes to Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Japan orders Cambodia evacuation planes to Thailand.

text.p: Japan on Friday decided to send three air force transport planes to Thailand in preparation for a possible evacuation operation from strife-torn Cambodia.
Top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said the three C-130 Hercules transport planes would leave as soon as preparations were complete.
He did not specify if the operation would involve just the evacuation of Japanese citizens.
Since fighting broke out between Cambodia's rival factions last weekend, one Japanese engineer has died in the conflict when he was caught in the crossfire.
Japan is Cambodia's biggest aid donor and has been actively engaged in diplomatic efforts to end the fighting in the country.
"This is a precautionary measure and does not mean that the situation in Cambodia has changed," Kajiyama told a news conference. "It is just better to be as close as possible to the action."
He said negotiations were underway with the Thai government on the timing of the arrival of the planes.
The three planes have been on standby since Wednesday on Japan's southernmost island of Okinawa, which is the closest jumping off point from Japan for a flight to Cambodia.
From Okinawa, a flight would take about six hours to Cambodia, far longer than a flight from Thailand which borders Cambodia.
Kajiyama said the planes would fly to Thailand's U-tapao airbase, about 200 km (130 miles) east of Bangkok.
There are still about 370 Japanese in Cambodia, of which 99 are tourists and the rest either aid workers or business people living there.
Former Japanese ambassador to Cambodia Yukio Imagawa said on Friday that pressure from the world community would not help resolve the turmoil in Cambodia.
"It is Cambodia's domestic political issue and it is in no sense an international issue," Imagawa told a news conference.
"Pressure from the international community will not be effective," said Imagawa, who visited Phnom Penh last month as Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's special envoy.

Cambodia's unwieldy coalition government collapsed in violence on Saturday when Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's forces moved against rival First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's men in the capital. Ranariddh had left the country the previous day.
The United States announced on Thursday it was suspending its aid programme for Cambodia for at least 30 days in response to Hun Sen's ouster of Ranariddh.
Germany also said it had suspended its aid and Australia said it was reviewing its policy.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) said on Thursday it still recognised Ranariddh as co-premier and it was delaying Cambodia's entry into the grouping indefinitely.

Cambodia was due to become a full member of ASEAN at the end of the month. ASEAN currently groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. Burma and Laos will become members later this month.
